Title: Man allegedly behind 'targeted' attack on Australian lawmaker due in court
Article:
WANGARATTA: The man alleged to have critically wounded Australian lawmaker Helen Haines in a "targeted" attack was due to appear in court on Wednesday, as police warned that growing extremism online was fuelling political polarisation.
Haines is in a "critical but stable condition" in a Melbourne hospital after being struck by a car on Monday near her office in Wangaratta, just over 200km northeast of the Victoria state capital, police said on Wednesday.
Police have charged 43-year-old Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of harming a public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
He is due to appear in court in Wangaratta on Wednesday.
The attack has prompted soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare, but where police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed at elected officials in recent years.
The alleged attacker's motive remains unknown, and authorities have refused to speculate while the investigation is ongoing.
However, police said on Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including whether he may have held radical anti-government views.
"Like everyone, we're examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues," Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush told journalists.
Australian Federal Police (AFP) Commissioner Krissy Barrett said there was a growing level of "extremist views" online.
"The current criminal threat environment is febrile, and when it comes to federal parliamentarians, the AFP continues to record the growing volume of online abuse, threatening rhetoric, and intimidation," she said.
[[nid:1560185]]
Soul-searching
The independent lawmaker, 65, was standing near the boot of her car when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on Monday afternoon.
Local media reported that she had undergone surgery, lost one of her legs and was fighting to save the other.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led an outpouring of support for Haines, who has been widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.
He has also lamented that political debate in Australia has become too heated and personal in recent years.
"It's important in a democracy that people are allowed to have disagreements," he said.
"But that doesn't mean that you have to draw into question people's motivations or their patriotism or who they are."
"We've seen, I think, political discourse go in the wrong direction in recent times," he said.
Australia's spy agency chief, Mike Burgess, warned after the alleged attack that "elevated levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation continue to create a permissive environment of violence".
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for positions such as supporting stronger climate action.

Title: Musk: SpaceX and Tesla's Terafab targets 2028 for volume chip production
Article:
SAN FRANCISCO: The chip manufacturing joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla called Terafab aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Elon Musk said on a SpaceX conference call on Tuesday.
"I put big error bars on this because we don't know if we will actually achieve this or not," Musk said, referring to the timeline.
The timeline is a rough schedule for a project that aims to produce 1 terawatt a year of computing power for AI and robotics, on a schedule Musk himself called "very aggressive."
In the United States, cutting-edge logic factories can take three or more years to build.
Musk has described the planned complex in Texas as combining advanced manufacturing, packaging and testing of both advanced logic and memory chips in one facility.
On Tuesday, Musk said that internally, Terafab aims to have a first test chip, using static random-access memory (SRAM) circuits, functional in roughly May or June of next year at the Terafab research facility in Austin.
Chip manufacturers commonly fabricate SRAM circuits as a method of refining manufacturing process development.
Musk cautions on ambitious dates
Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed. The SpaceX CEO described the Terafab timeline as the company's aspiration and said the dates are "very aggressive."
"Let's just say that outcome of achieving volume production is at least in the set of possible outcomes for Q3 or Q4 of '28," Musk said.
"So these are obviously like insanely fast time frames for chip  production."
Equipment acquisition challenge
On the SpaceX conference call, a sell-side analyst asked Musk whether SpaceX had placed orders for the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines produced only by the Dutch company ASML.
The EUV machines are necessary to produce the most cutting-edge chips made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices.
Musk did not answer the question directly and said, "Now these were very aggressive dates, and we're very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome."
One of the challenges Terafab faces is acquiring enough of the complex, expensive semiconductor manufacturing equipment from ASML or American suppliers such as Applied Materials and KLA.
Intel said in April that it would join the Terafab project to help accelerate Terafab's goals. Intel also posted ‌a photo of CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Musk shaking hands, saying it hosted the world's richest man at its campus that month.
The companies have not revealed how the collaboration would function in practice.
Earlier this month, Musk said there had been discussions about potential cooperation with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's largest advanced chip manufacturer.
But Musk later said Terafab is committed to running the facility itself. — REUTERS

Title: BBC slashes 100 jobs, closes two channels
Article:
LONDON: The BBC announced more than 100 job cuts and the closure of two channels on Tuesday as the cash-strapped UK broadcaster seeks to save £500 million (US$668 million) over the next two years.
BBC News announced the "net closure of just over 100 roles", according to an internal note by director Rachel Jupp, as part of some 2,000 job cuts the wider organisation is considering to achieve its planned savings.
The job cuts represent £5.5 million in savings, Jupp said in the note sent to AFP.
She was appointed BBC News director this month after her predecessor stepped down amid a row over a misleading edit of US President Donald Trump in a BBC documentary last year.
The BBC also said it would end broadcasts on BBC Scotland and BBC Three, a youth-oriented channel, with both remaining available on its online iPlayer streaming platform.
It also announced the closure of Radio 4 Extra, with its mainly archive-based programmes to be made available on BBC Sounds, an audio-streaming platform.
"We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices," BBC director-general Matt Brittin said in a note to staff.
"Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy it on iPlayer and Sounds," added the former Google executive, who took the helm of the BBC earlier this year.
Scottish Culture Minister Mairi McAllan said moving BBC Scotland online was "wholly unacceptable".
In June, the BBC announced plans to cut another 550 roles in its news, nations and content teams by the end of this financial year to deliver £160 million in savings.
The cuts come amid severe cost pressures after income from a licence fee that largely funds the corporation fell by around a quarter in real terms since 2017.
The broadcaster, which says 94 per cent of UK adults use its services monthly, has also been hit by a series of controversies and scandals in recent years that have undermined public confidence in it.
"The way people consume news is changing rapidly, and too many audiences, particularly younger audiences, are not finding us," Jupp said in her message.
Jupp added that BBC News could be required to make greater savings than anticipated: "Given the BBC's financial pressures, the savings requirement for News could increase."
Earlier this year, the BBC said it planned to save £500 million from its roughly £5 billion annual budget over the next three years by cutting up to 2,000 jobs, in its biggest round of redundancies since 2011.

Title: Netflix shares drop on slowing engagement, revenue growth
Article:
SAN FRANCISCO: Netflix shares fell more than five per cent on Tuesday afternoon after its quarterly earnings report failed to ease investor concerns about slowing viewer engagement and revenue growth.
"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," the company said in a letter to investors, referring to how it measures engagement, adding that it was "confident" it could accelerate that growth.
The California-based streaming giant has struggled to meet investor expectations for several quarters as it faces competition from other streaming services, gaming and sports.
Netflix "has underperformed significantly over the last 6-12 months", and investors are concerned "about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes", John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told AFP in a statement.
In its third quarter, which ended in September, Netflix recorded US$12.87 billion in revenue and US$3.7 billion in net income, above investor expectations, according to FactSet.
It did not provide overall figures for subscriber viewing hours during the quarter, but noted that the metric increased 24 per cent in India compared with the same period last year.
In July, Netflix said subscribers had spent 97 billion hours watching content in the first half of the year, a two per cent increase from the first half of 2025.
It stopped reporting subscriber numbers in the first half of 2025.
However, the company touted growth outside the US while acknowledging challenges in its home market.
"We do need better execution in the US. Our content around the world is largely working," co-chief executive Ted Sarandos told investors on an analyst call on Tuesday, highlighting engagement, subscribers, revenue and profits across Latin America, Europe and Asia.
"The US is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos added.
Job cuts
The company will also reportedly cut around six per cent of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, according to media reports.
Among those affected were seven senior employees responsible for television deals and content, The Hollywood Reporter reported last week.
The company also recently replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria, who oversaw popular shows including "Stranger Things", "Bridgerton" and "Squid Game", while also driving the company's live entertainment strategy, according to CNBC.
Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as its new content chief.
"Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work," Sarandos said on Tuesday's call.
Diverse formats
Competition from other streaming services has forced Netflix to work harder to attract and retain both paying and ad-supported subscribers.
The company has increasingly ventured into live sports, with agreements to stream major events such as the Olympics and World Cup, alongside gaming and shorter-form content. The NFL and WWE have also signed on to stream live events.
In the US, Netflix accounted for 7.8 per cent of streaming television viewership in July, compared with YouTube's 14.2 per cent, a record for the Google-owned platform, according to media analytics firm Nielsen.
The World Cup boosted overall television viewership in July, according to Nielsen.
"It's really important to remember, roughly 95 per cent of our spend and nearly all of our revenue is focused on that core, where we see a long runway for future growth," Sarandos said on Tuesday's call, emphasising the company's commitment to traditional television and film content.
The company also fell short of expectations for advertising revenue growth.
"We are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year. We're still growing" in advertising, co-chief executive Greg Peters said on the call.
"We see the benefits when we continue to roll out other products like new ad formats, which help with our growth," Peters added.

Title: Trump says he wants Zelenskyy to 'make a deal' with Russia
Article:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday urged Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal with Russia, increasing pressure on the Ukrainian leader even as Moscow continues its war, launched four years ago.
Trump also said he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Moscow's forces years earlier in Ukraine, in a fresh sign of his shift back towards Moscow.
"We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," Trump told reporters in the same room.
Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and Zelenskyy had a bruising televised confrontation in the Oval Office in February 2025, shortly after the Ukraine-sceptic US president returned to office.
"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump said on Tuesday.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel supply deal with Putin and criticised Zelenskyy as a warmonger over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The Ukrainian leader met Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday for talks aimed at easing tensions.
Zelenskyy welcomed the resumption of US intelligence-sharing on impending Russian strikes but insisted that Kyiv must be included in any future talks on its fate, following meetings with US envoys.
Ukraine has become increasingly alarmed by Trump's return to effectively blaming Kyiv for the failure to end the war that began with Moscow's invasion in February 2022, as well as his warm words towards Putin.
Trump indicated that a deal with Russia to free Hubbard could be imminent.
"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said in response to a question from an AFP journalist.
"Just stick with me," Trump added. "Just you remember that question a couple of days from now, because I do things that nobody else can do."

Title: Experts: It could be gloves off between Pas and Bersatu in Melaka [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   Open hostility between Pas and Bersatu could play out in the Melaka polls, now that the deregistration of Perikatan Nasional has removed the last thing holding the former partners back.
International Islamic University Malaysia political scientist Associate Professor Dr Syaza Shukri said the two parties had previously held back from conflict.
"They've already clashed in Johor and Negri Sembilan, but previously, they were trying to defend their cooperation in PN.
"Pas has been clear about not working with Bersatu. So now, Bersatu can retaliate," she said.
She said Bersatu stood to lose the most as its logo was less known to voters.
"We always hear that voters on the ground don't know Bersatu's logo. During the Negri Sembilan election, people were asking what the party with the
bunga raya
logo was."
Fence-sitters, however, were unlikely to be thrown by PN's absence, as they could still identify with Pas, she said.
"It might be confusing, because they may be looking for the main coalitions: Pakatan Harapan, Barisan Nasional and PN. But when they see Pas, I think they can connect the dots," she said.
Meanwhile, Institute for Democracy and Economic
Affairs  chief executive officer Aira Azhari said Pas would need allies to stay competitive in Melaka and avoid splitting the Malay vote.
"Electorally, they do not have a history of performing well in Melaka, so they will need to form some kind of pact."
She said while Pas' well-recognised brand gave it an edge over its former partners, going solo would cost it non-Malay support.
"Pas running on its own means it is very unlikely to get non-Malay votes."
Aira said the deregistration might push Pas, Bersatu, Wawasan and Gerakan to recalibrate, either by forming a new coalition or alliances with each other.
However, Syaza said the move could be a blessing in disguise in that it would allow all parties to start afresh.
She said smaller parties such as Wawasan, Pejuang and possibly Gerakan could even thrive by contesting under the Pas logo, much like PH's component parties did under PKR's logo in the 2018 General Election.
"Of course, a registered coalition is better for future planning, especially when it comes to the leadership issue, which, ironically, is what brought down PN."
The  Melaka assembly was dissolved on Sept 23 and polls will be held on Nov 14.
PN, formed in 2020 in the wake of the Sheraton Move, had its registration cancelled under subparagraph 13(1)(c)(iv) of the Societies Act 1966.
The Registry of Societies said the coalition's  representations on Oct 12 failed to refute the grounds for cancellation set out in its Sept 22 notice.
